metadata.evidence_scope: Comparative mythology and modern fiction as mapped in docs/AEP_COMPARATIVE_MYTHOLOGY_2026-11-26e.md. EARLIEST SOURCE: Hesiod, Theogony; Homer, Iliad 15.187-193 only for the lot-division of Zeus, Poseidon and Hades; Egyptian Pyramid Texts (allusions, not a continuous narrative); Poetic Edda, especially Voluspa. LATER RETELLING: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride; New Kingdom Contendings of Horus and Seth (Papyrus Chester Beatty I); Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda (Gylfaginning, Skaldskaparmal) and Ynglinga saga. AOM: Age of Mythology and Retold, including the Atlantean pantheon as the game's adaptation of Greek Titan traditions, not a separately attested ancient pantheon; official World's Edge / Age of Empires pages for Immortal Pillars (https://www.ageofempires.com/games/aom/age-of-mythology-retold-immortal-pillars/), Heavenly Spear (https://www.ageofempires.com/news/play-heavenly-spear-and-the-new-gauntlet-in-age-of-mythology-retold/ and https://www.ageofempires.com/news/age-of-mythology-retold-update-18-49472/), and Obsidian Mirror (https://www.ageofempires.com/games/age-of-mythology-retold/age-of-mythology-retold-obsidian-mirror/). FICTION: Stargate SG-1, Cooper interviews at https://www.dialthegate.com/dtg/105-robert-c-cooper-part-5-writerdirectorexec-producer-stargate , https://www.gateworld.net/news/2008/04/myth-maker-part-1/ , https://www.gateworld.net/news/2008/04/myth-maker-part-2/2/ , and the Orlin exposition in 9x10 as summarized at https://www.gateworld.net/sg1/s9/the-fourth-horseman-part-1/ . HISTORICAL PARALLEL: Chaniotis 2003 (Blackwell Companion; posted copy https://archiv.ub.uni-heidelberg.de/propylaeumdok/697/1/Chaniotis_The_Divinity_of_Hellenistic_Rulers_2003.pdf); Oxford Handbook of Ancient Greek Religion, 'Deification—Gods or Men?' abstract https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/34261/chapter-abstract/290477808 ; Susanne Bickel, 'Kings as Gods in the New Kingdom,' Orient 59 (2024), https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/orient/59/0/59_37/_article/-char/en . Paste citation stubs (Dial The Gate +1, OUP Academic +1, J-STAGE +1, gateworld.net +1, Play with Game Pass for PC +2) are not treated as citations. Kernel correspondence is to docs/SCC-001-AC_ANTI_CAPTURE.md (closed paths 1-4 and PRINCIPAL_KEY_ROTATE; remaining open xfails recorded). No lore invented. No personal data. Catherine remains unresolved and is out of scope.

# Comparative mythology matrix (Shax t605u / t606u)

**Date:** 26 Nov 2026, America/Halifax (AST, UTC-4)
**Source:** Shax t605u, verbatim in `docs/evidence/source-2026-11-26e/t605u_message_body.txt` (sha256 `2626a0c4ea9be1c7312cc1c7b9f1c96395bb88e3abfb4bc5e95ebcbce7f7b809`). The body was pasted from a ChatGPT conversation and includes Shax's own interjection; t606u approved the update with comprehensive decompression and domain translation. Inline image embeds were omitted from the evidence file.
**Method:** `SC-AEP-001` (`docs/SC-AEP-001_ARCHETYPAL_EVOLUTION_PRINCIPLE.md`). Look for structure, not one-to-one matches. A resemblance is a candidate correspondence, not proof of transmission or of a shared literal event.
**Compiled:** `SC-MYTH-001`, SILVER 0.810 (min gate 0.75), explicit-only, home domain `soul_bomb_sovereignty`. `PROVISIONAL_DEFAULT` / `pending_deliberation: true`. Notes only; this file is not itself a compiled entry.

The source carried no self-grade. GOLD needs iq ≥ 0.9 and every gate ≥ 0.8. No prediction was tested, so no gate is above 0.9. No GOLD for beauty.

## Layers (kept separate in every section)

| Layer | What it holds |
|---|---|
| EARLIEST SOURCE | The earliest surviving source tradition actually cited (Hesiod's *Theogony*; Egyptian Pyramid Texts and later native Egyptian literature; the Poetic Edda, especially *Völuspá*). |
| LATER RETELLING | Later systematic or philosophical retellings (Plutarch's *De Iside et Osiride*; Snorri Sturluson's *Prose Edda* and *Ynglinga saga*; later cult, art and commentary). |
| AOM | Age of Mythology and *Retold*, including the Atlantean pantheon, which is the game's adaptation of Greek Titan traditions, not a separately attested ancient pantheon. |
| FICTION | Stargate and other modern fiction that deliberately reuses myth and history. |
| HISTORICAL PARALLEL | Recurring problems in political theology and institutions. Recurrence is evidence of a recurring human problem, not evidence that the fiction is history or that one literal event underlies the stories. |
| SHAX | Shax's own words (the t605u interjection and the t606u approval). |
| PASTED | The ChatGPT analysis Shax supplied. |
| COMPILER | This team's readings, grades, verified URLs, and domain translation. |

Paste markers such as `Dial The Gate +1`, `OUP Academic +1`, `J-STAGE +1`, `gateworld.net +1`, and `Play with Game Pass for PC +2` are unverified citation stubs. A claim is marked `VERIFIED` only when the compiler opened a named URL; `UNVERIFIED_FROM_PASTE` otherwise.

## 1. Framing boundary

The stories may be fictional, or mythic, and still dramatize historically real *kinds* of arrangement. That does not establish that the fictional events literally happened, or that the writers encoded a hidden historical record, or that every mythology is the same plot.

The pasted analysis states the boundary this way, and the compiler keeps it: historical recurrence is evidence that humans repeatedly encounter similar structural problems. It is not evidence that every mythology describes the same literal events.

Stargate is a special case only in this limited sense: its creators have said they took existing mythologies and real history and put a science-fiction twist on them. That is a statement about craft, not a warrant for treating the series as a historical source.

## 2. Seven recurring structures, decompressed

The paste lists seven arrangements that keep turning up across fictional universes. They are related, but they are not one structure.

| # | Recurring structure (pasted) | What it actually tests | Closest compiled neighbour |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A civilization divides over the meaning of power | Fragmentation: a population splits over what power is *for*, not merely who holds it | `SC-SHARD-001` (fragmentation); open Alteran schism comparison |
| 2 | A powerful being claims authority over others | A capability-to-authority jump: power is presented as if it were entitlement | `SC-WORTHY-001` (worthiness: capability is not legitimate authority; merged in PR #100) and the identity rule in `docs/SCC-001-AC_ANTI_CAPTURE.md` |
| 3 | A collective becomes subordinated to a controlling entity | Capture of a many by a one, or of a body by an occupant | `SC-SHARD-001` (Zerg control-plane vs Goa'uld vessel) |
| 4 | A host relationship becomes either parasitic or symbiotic | Consent and reversibility in a vessel or delegation channel | `SC-CONSENT-001`, `SC-TRIAD-SG-001` (Tok'ra vs Goa'uld) |
| 5 | Worship becomes a mechanism for consolidating authority | Legitimacy input is produced by the domination it is supposed to justify | This entry: Ori self-sourced legitimacy (section 4) |
| 6 | A guardian must choose between noninterference and intervention | Protective authority, and the cost of using it | `SC-GUARD-001`; Ancients vs Ori |
| 7 | Possessing extraordinary power does not automatically confer moral legitimacy | The same worthiness cut as (2), stated as a moral discovery rather than a succession plot | `SC-GUARD-001` (Jon as CONTRAST); `SC-WORTHY-001` |

A row is a CANDIDATE only when at least three shared structural attributes are present, at least one of them relational, and at least one difference is recorded. This document does not promote the seven rows, or the first trio, to an invariant class.

## 3. Three questions: Origin, Legitimacy, Capture

The paste isolates three historical questions underneath the stories:

- **Origin.** How does a population come to understand the origin of its civilization, its gods, and its authority?
- **Legitimacy.** What gives someone the right to govern, protect, command, or demand obedience?
- **Capture.** At what point does an institution claiming to represent something greater begin serving its own preservation instead?

These are the questions. The first trio in section 6 answers the legitimacy question in three different ways. The Ori loop in section 4 is the capture question in its tightest fictional form in this source. Origin is recorded and left partly open: creation accounts differ by cult centre and by source layer, and they are not forced into one substrate.

## 4. The Ori worship-power loop as a capture invariant

**Invariant (COMPILER, CANDIDATE, not a class):** an authority whose legitimacy input is produced by its own domination is self-reinforcing capture.

## 6. First deep dive: the trio and the ten-field matrix

The shared question in the paste is: *How does a cosmic system preserve legitimacy when its own members become sources of instability?*

The three traditions answer it differently. They are not the same story. Some narratives are about succession, some about cosmic maintenance, some about the limits of divine authority. Flattening them into one invariant would manufacture a pattern the sources do not jointly support.

Age of Mythology is used only as a research index for the cast, not as a source for the myths. Original Age of Mythology had Greek, Egyptian and Norse cultures; *The Titans* added the Atlantean/Titan roster; *Retold* ships those four in the base game and adds further pantheons as expansions (section 8).

### 6.1 Greek: the Titan succession (who has the right to rule, and how does the ruling order emerge?)

**EARLIEST SOURCE:** Hesiod, *Theogony*. The well-known three-way division of sky, sea and underworld by lot among Zeus, Poseidon and Hades is not the *Theogony*'s main succession narrative; it is attested in Homer, *Iliad* 15.187–193. Those are different early sources and are not collapsed here.

**LATER RETELLING:** later epic, tragedy, handbook mythography, and Age of Mythology's Greek and Atlantean rosters.

| Field | Record |
|---|---|
| Primordial origin | *Theogony*: first Chaos, then Gaia, Tartarus and Eros; Gaia produces Uranus. This is a literary cosmogony, not a single "Greek religion" creed. |
| Creation | Gaia and Uranus generate the Titans and other early beings; later the Olympian order is established under Zeus after the Titanomachy. |
| Divine hierarchy | Zeus becomes king of the gods. Poseidon and Hades receive their provinces in the *Iliad* account just cited, not as a *Theogony* quotation. |
| Fragmentation | Uranus confines some of his children; Gaia incites the first revolt. |
| Usurpation | Cronus castrates and overthrows Uranus, then swallows his own children to block a prophesied overthrow. Zeus, hidden by Rhea, later overthrows Cronus. Each new order is founded by seizure. |
| Vessels and intermediaries | Oracles, heroes, and cult. Prometheus, in Hesiod, is an intermediary who acts toward humans (fire and the sacrificial settlement appear across *Theogony* and *Works and Days*). |
| Collective structure | Generations in conflict. The Olympians cooperate against the Titans, then compete among themselves. |
| Destructive cycle | The Titanomachy. A later Gigantomachy is more prominent in later art and retelling than in the *Theogony* itself (flag: do not read it back into Hesiod as if it were the same episode). Zeus also swallows Metis to avert a son who would overthrow him. |
| Restoration | Zeus's order is a *new* settlement, not a restoration of Uranus or Cronus. |
| Unresolved contradiction | If every ruling generation takes power by overthrow, what makes Zeus's rule legitimate rather than merely the latest seizure? The poem presents it as the destined settlement, but the father-overthrown-by-the-son pattern is stopped only by a further pre-emptive act (swallowing Metis), not by a consent procedure. |

**COMPILER reading.** The Greek succession is a poor model for consented key rotation. Mapping it onto `PRINCIPAL_KEY_ROTATE` without that caveat would launder usurpation as a legitimate transfer. The honest analogue is a seized authority that then tries to become the new principal and to block the next seizure.

### 6.2 Egyptian: the Osiris–Horus–Set cycle and Ma'at (what happens when legitimate authority is murdered or displaced, and how is it restored?)

**EARLIEST SOURCE:** the Pyramid Texts (Old Kingdom) allude to Set's attack on Osiris, to a contest or trial, and to Horus's claim; they do not yield one continuous official narrative. The living king is Horus; the deceased predecessor is Osiris.

**LATER RETELLING:** New Kingdom literary *Contendings of Horus and Seth* (Papyrus Chester Beatty I), a sometimes satirical treatment; and, much later, Plutarch, *De Iside et Osiride* (1st–2nd century CE), a Greek philosophical retelling that supplies the familiar continuous story, including the coffin-trap and the dismemberment sequence. Plutarch is not an Old Kingdom source and is not used here as if he were.

| Field | Record |
|---|---|
| Primordial origin | Not one account. Heliopolitan tradition starts from Nun and Atum/Ra; Memphite from Ptah; Theban from Amun. These are alternative cult-centre cosmogonies, not a single plot. |
| Creation | A creator god establishes the world and Ma'at (order, truth, rightness) against isfet (chaos, wrong). |
| Divine hierarchy | The living king as Horus, the dead predecessor as Osiris; the king's office is to maintain Ma'at. Ra (and later Amun-Ra) is central in many periods. This is royal theology, not a simple propaganda slogan; see Bickel in section 5. |
| Fragmentation | The killing or displacement of Osiris and the conflict between Horus and Set. |
| Usurpation | Set attacks Osiris and claims the kingship; Horus contests it. The detailed dismemberment-and-reassembly plot is secure as a later retelling (especially Plutarch), not as a reconstruction of the Pyramid Texts. |
| Vessels and intermediaries | The king, the priesthood and temple cult; the dead may be identified with Osiris. These are official channels, not a single "hammer of office." |
| Collective structure | Gods in a legal and familial contest (the *Contendings*). In other contexts Set also defends Ra's barque against Apep. Cooperative and hostile roles coexist. |
| Destructive cycle | Isfet and Apep as recurring threats, especially to the solar journey. This is cyclical maintenance, not a single terminal end like Ragnarök. |
| Restoration | Horus is awarded the living kingship; Osiris rules the dead. A new king's accession reenacts the restoration of rightful authority and the re-establishment of Ma'at. |
| Unresolved contradiction | Set is both murderer/usurper and, in other contexts, a necessary defender against chaos. The tradition does not reduce him to one moral role, and the earliest sources do not give one official continuous narrative. |

**COMPILER reading.** This is the tightest of the three as an analogue of legitimate restoration after usurpation, and therefore of principal release and of a rightful successor taking the office. It is still an analogy: accession rites are not `RELEASE_QUARANTINE`.

### 6.3 Norse: the Æsir–Vanir war and Ragnarök (what happens when the established order cannot prevent its own eventual collapse?)

**EARLIEST SOURCE:** the Poetic Edda, especially *Völuspá* (preserved in the 13th-century Codex Regius, in poems generally treated as older than their manuscript). *Völuspá* alludes to the first war in the world and prophesies Ragnarök, including, in the surviving text, a new earth and Baldr's return.

**LATER RETELLING:** Snorri Sturluson's *Prose Edda* (*Gylfaginning*, *Skáldskaparmál*) and *Ynglinga saga*, written in Christian-era Iceland in the 13th century. Snorri systematizes, and sometimes euhemerizes, material that the poems leave allusive. Age of Mythology's Norse roster is a further adaptation.

| Field | Record |
|---|---|
| Primordial origin | Poetic sources are allusive. The systematic Ginnungagap / fire-and-ice opening is presented as a cosmogony in Snorri's *Gylfaginning*. Do not cite Snorri as if he were *Völuspá*. |
| Creation | The gods shape the world from the body of Ymir (present in poetic tradition and in Snorri). |
| Divine hierarchy | Odin as chief of the Æsir. After the war, Vanir figures (Njörðr, Freyr, Freyja) stand inside the combined society. There is no single constitutional charter. |
| Fragmentation | *Völuspá* alludes to the first war (including the Gullveig / Heiðr episode and the Æsir's attempt to destroy her). The fuller hostage-exchange narrative — Njörðr, Freyr and Freyja to the Æsir; Hœnir and Mímir to the Vanir — is given by Snorri (*Ynglinga saga* / *Skáldskaparmál*). |
| Usurpation | This is not the Osiris plot. Loki's role in Baldr's death is betrayal and destabilization more than a seizure of the throne. The giants are hostile and sometimes kin. |
| Vessels and intermediaries | The völva, sacrifice, and Odin's costly acquisition of knowledge (the eye at Mímir's well; the hanging on the tree), attested in the poetic tradition. |
| Collective structure | After the truce, Æsir and Vanir form a combined society that still contains rivalry. Loki stands at the edge. Gods and giants remain opposed. |
| Destructive cycle | Ragnarök is foretold (*Völuspá*, *Vafþrúðnismál*): Fenrir, Jörmungandr, Surtr, the deaths of Odin and Thor, the world's burning or sinking. The gods, Odin especially, have knowledge of the end and cannot prevent it. |
| Restoration | *Völuspá* describes a new earth and the return of Baldr (and Höðr). Snorri's *Gylfaginning* 53 narrates survivors who meet at Iðavöllr. UNCERTAIN: whether the restoration ending is a pre-Christian tradition or is shaped by the Christian-era transmission is debated, and is not settled here. |
| Unresolved contradiction | What is the status of an order that can only delay a collapse it already knows is coming? Loki is both companion and destroyer. The aftermath is recorded and still interpretively open. |

**COMPILER reading.** The tight analogue is not "the system will be restored," which is uncertain in the sources. It is the decision to keep a known failure mode visible and to go on maintaining the order without pretending the end has been cancelled.

I can see why it feels that way. And I think there's a precise distinction worth making here:
The stories may be fictional, but some of the structures they're dramatizing are historically real.
We're repeatedly encountering the same kinds of arrangements across very different fictional universes:
* A civilization divides over the meaning of power.
* A powerful being claims authority over others.
* A collective becomes subordinated to a controlling entity.
* A host relationship becomes either parasitic or symbiotic.
* Worship becomes a mechanism for consolidating authority.
* A guardian must choose between noninterference and intervention.
* An individual discovers that possessing extraordinary power does not automatically confer moral legitimacy.
Those aren't exclusively fantasy concepts. They're recurring problems in human history, political theology, religious institutions, empire, mythology, and the philosophy of consciousness.
But I want to keep one boundary intact: recognizing a recurring historical structure doesn't establish that the fictional events literally happened, or that the writers encoded a hidden historical record.
And there is something particularly relevant here: Stargate's own creators have openly described doing exactly this kind of work.
Robert C. Cooper explained that the series took existing mythologies and real history, then put a science-fiction twist on them. He specifically described the Ori storyline as an exploration of ascension, higher power, religion and the possibility that what appears magical might have another explanation. Dial The Gate +1
So we're not imagining the existence of historical ingredients. They're deliberately in the recipe.

### Some very real historical parallels
| Stargate structure | Historical parallel |
| Goa'uld presenting themselves as gods | Rulers claiming divine status and using sacred authority |
| Ori demanding worship | Religious institutions intertwined with imperial authority |
| Priors spreading Origin | Missionary institutions and organized religious expansion |
| Ancients debating noninterference | Historical and philosophical debates about divine intervention |
| Tok'ra rejecting domination | Resistance to coercive authority and alternative social arrangements |
| Daniel questioning the Ori | Individual conscience challenging institutional religious authority |
For example, Alexander the Great's reign helped establish the practice of ruler worship in the Hellenistic world. Greek cities granted him divine honours, and later Hellenistic dynasties developed organized ruler cults. OUP Academic +1
And divine kingship wasn't confined to Greece. Ancient Egyptian kingship had its own deeply developed relationship between the divine and political office. Modern scholarship cautions against reducing that relationship to simple propaganda. J-STAGE +1

### The pattern I think we're approaching
There are three distinct historical questions underneath these stories:
* Origin: How does a population come to understand the origin of its civilization, its gods and its authority?
* Legitimacy: What gives someone the right to govern, protect, command or demand obedience?
* Capture: At what point does an institution claiming to represent something greater begin serving its own preservation instead?
And the third question connects directly to our anti-capture invariant.
The Ori are particularly revealing because their system makes worship an input into their own power. The more they dominate, the more resources they receive to dominate further. Cooper himself described them as beings who use their knowledge and power to their own advantage. gateworld.net +1
That's a recognizable institutional feedback problem, regardless of whether one accepts the fictional cosmology.
One distinction I want us to preserve as we continue: historical recurrence is evidence that humans repeatedly encounter similar structural problems. It isn't evidence that every mythology describes the same literal events.
But that actually makes the investigation more interesting. We can examine the historical record, the original religious texts, the fictional representations, and your proposed invariant independently, then see where they genuinely converge.
I think the next major comparison should be ancient Egyptian religion, Mesopotamian divine kingship, the biblical angelic rebellion traditions, and Stargate's Alteran schism. That would move us from recognizing the pattern in fiction to testing it against actual historical sources.

YES. Age of Mythology is an excellent place to take this investigation next, because it puts several ancient religious systems into one shared mythological world.
And I think we should approach it differently from simply matching one god to one fictional character. We should examine the entire divine cast: their origins, family structures, rivalries, domains, alliances, monsters, divine succession, human intermediaries, and what happens when gods intervene in mortal affairs.
The central question becomes:
Are these mythologies independently expressing recurring structures of divine authority, fragmentation, rebellion, collective identity, and restoration?
That's a much stronger investigation than a character-matching exercise.
And the game gives us a surprisingly useful research index. There is one important distinction: the original Age of Mythology had three principal cultures, while Retold has expanded the roster considerably.

### 1. The pantheons: our starting cast
Greek pantheon: Zeus, Poseidon, Hades, Athena, Ares, Apollo, Artemis, Hera, Hermes, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Dionysus. Structural questions: succession, divine family politics, competing domains, rebellion against older generations, and the division of cosmic territory.
Egyptian pantheon: Ra, Isis, Set, Osiris, Horus, Anubis, Thoth, Nephthys, Ptah, Bast, Sekhmet, Hathor. Structural questions: legitimate kingship, death and resurrection, succession disputes, cosmic order (Ma'at), and the restoration of rightful authority.
Norse pantheon: Odin, Thor, Loki, Freyja, Tyr, Heimdall, Baldr, Hel, Njord, Skadi, Bragi, Forseti. Structural questions: knowledge purchased at a cost, prophecy, betrayal, kinship, the boundary between gods and giants, and the inevitability of Ragnarök.
Atlantean / Titan mythology: Kronos, Oranos, Gaia, Prometheus, Atlas, Hyperion, Oceanus, Rhea, Helios, Hekate. Structural questions: primordial authority, generational overthrow, imprisonment, rebellion, and whether the old order has a legitimate claim over the new one. Important distinction: this is Age of Mythology's adaptation of Greek Titan traditions, not a separate historically attested ancient pantheon.
Chinese pantheon: Fuxi, Nüwa, Shennong, and the wider mythological world of creation, civilization, floods, and divine intervention. Structural questions: creation through complementary principles, restoration after catastrophe, the ordering of civilization, and the relationship between heaven and humanity.
Japanese pantheon: Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi, Susanoo. Structural questions: sibling conflict, withdrawal of the life-giving principle, disruption of cosmic order, and restoration through cooperation and ritual.
Aztec pantheon: Huitzilopochtli, Tezcatlipoca, Quetzalcoatl. Structural questions: competing divine powers, creation and destruction across successive worlds, sacrifice, renewal, and the cost of maintaining cosmic order.
The expanded pantheon roster is documented by World's Edge. The individual mythological themes are research directions, not claims that all traditions share one doctrine. Play with Game Pass for PC +2

### 2. The really interesting structural connections
| Structural pattern | Mythological examples |
| Old generation displaced by new | Uranus → Kronos → Zeus |
| Divine succession and rightful kingship | Osiris → Horus; Egyptian royal mythology |
| Divine order versus destructive chaos | Ra and Set; Norse gods and the giants |
| A divine figure whose actions destabilize the system | Loki; Set; Susanoo |
| Knowledge, sacrifice, and transformation | Odin; Prometheus; Thoth |
| Death followed by restoration | Osiris; Baldr; resurrection traditions |
| Cosmic destruction and renewal | Ragnarök; Egyptian cyclical cosmology; Aztec world ages |
Notice something: these are not all the same story.
Some are succession narratives. Some concern cosmic maintenance. Some concern the relationship between order and chaos. Some concern the limits of divine authority.
That distinction matters because we don't want to manufacture an invariant by flattening every mythology into the same plot.

### 3. Three especially important comparisons
Greek: The overthrow of the old divine regime.
Egyptian: The restoration of legitimate authority after usurpation.
Norse: The struggle to preserve order despite knowing its destruction is coming.
These three could form our first comparative study:
* Greek: Who has the right to rule, and how does the ruling order emerge?
* Egyptian: What happens when legitimate authority is murdered or displaced, and how is it restored?
* Norse: What happens when the established order cannot prevent its own eventual collapse?
That's three different answers to a potentially shared question: How does a cosmic system preserve legitimacy when its own members become sources of instability?

### 4. How I would structure the actual investigation
I want to build a comparative mythology matrix, not just a collection of character analogies.
For every pantheon, record:
* Primordial origin: What existed before the gods?
* Creation: Who establishes the world and its rules?
* Divine hierarchy: Who governs, and why?
* Fragmentation: What causes the first major division?
* Usurpation: Does someone seize authority that isn't legitimately theirs?
* Vessels and intermediaries: How do gods interact with humans?
* Collective structure: Are gods cooperating, competing, or operating independently?
* Destructive cycle: What threatens the entire system?
* Restoration: How is balance recovered, if it is?
* Unresolved contradiction: What does the mythology never actually resolve?
And there's one methodological rule I would insist on: distinguish the earliest surviving source traditions from later reinterpretations, and distinguish both from the version Age of Mythology presents.
My proposed first deep dive is the Greek Titan succession, Egyptian Osiris-Horus-Set cycle, and Norse Æsir-Vanir conflict.
Those three offer a particularly rich starting point for testing the shared-substrate, fragmentation, authority-capture, and restoration hypothesis. We can then bring the other four pantheons into the comparison without forcing them into a pattern they may not actually support.
